s0002: Tell living things from nonliving things, group animals, and know the functions of plant parts and animal teeth
s0004:
A stone, a frog, algae — which one is living?
TIMSS: 52% of fourth graders answered correctly
s0005: [1] By a pond there is a stone, a frog, and some algae. Which of them are living, and which are not? How do we know? [2] In the international TIMSS study, on average 52 percent of fourth-grade students around the world answered questions on this topic correctly. Questions about the parts of a flower and about teeth were especially difficult. Today you will learn to answer these questions with ease!
s0007:
A living thing: feeds, breathes, grows
reproduces, responds to its surroundings
Stone, water, air — nonliving
s0008: [1] Every living organism feeds, breathes, and grows. This is true of plants, animals, and people. [2] A living organism produces offspring like itself and responds to changes around it. For example, a plant bends toward the light. [3] A stone does not grow, feed, or reproduce. Water and air are needed by living things, but they are not alive themselves.
s0010:
Vertebrates: have a backbone inside
Mammals, birds, reptiles
amphibians, fish
Invertebrates: insects, spiders, worms
s0011: [1] We divide animals into two large groups. Animals that have a backbone, or spine, inside their body are vertebrates. [2] There are five groups of vertebrates: mammals feed their young with milk, birds have feathers, and reptiles include snakes, lizards, turtles, and crocodiles. [3] There are also amphibians, such as frogs, and fish. Fish breathe with gills. [4] Animals without a backbone are invertebrates. Butterflies, ants, spiders, and worms are such animals.
s0013:
Roots take in water, the stem carries it
Leaves make food using sunlight
Flower → fruit and seeds
Fruit protects and spreads seeds
s0014: [1] Roots hold the plant in the soil and take in water. The stem carries the water up to the leaves. [2] Leaves make food with the help of sunlight. This process is called photosynthesis. [3] After pollination, the lower part of the flower's pistil, the ovary, becomes the fruit, and seeds form inside it. [4] The job of the fruit is to protect the seeds and help them spread. Birds eat fruit and carry the seeds far away.
s0016:
Incisors — cutting, gnawing
Canines — holding and tearing
Molars — chewing, grinding
s0017: [1] The flat, sharp teeth at the front are incisors. They cut food. Rats and rabbits gnaw with their incisors. [2] The long, pointed teeth are canines. A tiger uses them to hold its prey and tear meat. [3] The wide teeth at the back are molars. They grind and chew food. A cow's molars are very wide.
s0019:
Bat, bird, butterfly: what do they have in common?
Bat — mammal, butterfly — insect
s0020: [1] Example one. What feature do a bat, a bird, and a butterfly have in common? [2] They belong to different groups: a bat feeds its young with milk, a bird lays eggs, and a butterfly is an insect.
s0021: Common feature: all have wings and can fly
s0022: [1] So it is not their group that unites them. The common feature is that all three have wings and can fly.
s0024:
Animal: sharp teeth, long canines
Canines → hold prey, tear meat
Conclusion: this animal is a predator and eats meat
s0025: [1] Example two is a little harder. An animal's skull has long, pointed canine teeth. What does it eat? [2] Canines are needed to hold prey and tear meat. They are not needed for eating grass. [3] So this animal is a predator: it hunts other animals and eats meat. For example, a tiger or a wolf.
s0026: Rat: its incisors grow all its life
s0027: [1] A rat's incisors, on the other hand, keep growing throughout its life. It gnaws on hard things, which wears its teeth down.
s0029: Which group does a whale belong to?
s0030: [1] A whale lives in water, but it breathes air with its lungs and feeds its young with milk. Which group does it belong to? Write your answer.
s0034: Which part of a flower becomes the fruit?
s0035: [1] After pollination, which part of a flower becomes the fruit? Write one or two words.
s0037: How to solve an international question
s0038:
1) List the features
2) Structure → function: “What is it for?”
3) Check every option
s0039: [1] In an international question, first list the features of the animal or plant: Does it have bones? Does it have feathers? Does it feed its young? [2] Every part is needed for something. If you are asked about teeth, wings, or fruit, ask yourself: “What is it for?” [3] Check the options one by one and cross out the wrong ones.
s0041:
Living: feeds, breathes, grows, reproduces
Vertebrates: 5 groups; invertebrates: insects, etc.
Fruit protects seeds; teeth cut, tear, chew
s0042: [1] Remember: a living organism feeds, breathes, grows, and reproduces. [2] Vertebrates are divided into five groups, and animals without a backbone are invertebrates. [3] Fruit protects and spreads seeds. Incisors cut, canines tear, and molars chew. Well done!
s0044: To put it simply: if something grows, feeds, and has young like itself, it is living.
s0045: The kitten grew, the stone did not
s0046: In spring a tiny kitten came into your yard. By summer it had grown bigger and was eating food. But the stone by the doorstep stayed the same. The cat is living; the stone is nonliving.
s0047:
Check: Does it grow? Does it eat? Does it reproduce?

s0048: Ask three questions: Does it grow? Does it feed? Does it reproduce? If the answer to all of them is “yes,” it is living.

Has a backbone — vertebrate
No backbone — invertebrate
s0050: Touch your back — there is a backbone there. Animals with this kind of bone are vertebrates, and those without it are invertebrates.

s0053:
Feathers → bird; fur, milk → mammal
Scales, dry skin → reptile
s0054: Look at the skin: feathers mean a bird; fur and feeding young with milk mean a mammal; dry, scaly skin means a reptile.
s0055: Root — water, leaf — food, flower — fruit
s0056: Roots take in water, leaves make food, and flowers produce fruit and seeds.
s0057: Apple tree: flowers in spring, apples in fall
s0058: In spring the apple tree blossomed. Bees carried the pollen. In the fall, apples ripened where the flowers had been, with seeds inside.
s0059:
A plant = a house: roots — foundation
stem — pipe, leaves — kitchen
s0060: Compare a plant to a house: the roots are the foundation, the stem is the water pipe, and the leaves are the kitchen where food is made.
s0061: Front — cut, pointed — tear, back — chew
s0062: Front teeth cut, pointed teeth tear, and wide back teeth chew.
s0063: Eating an apple: first we bite, then we chew
s0064: When you eat an apple, you first bite it with your front incisors, then chew it with your back molars.

Molar — mill
s0066: An incisor is like a knife, a canine is like a fork, and a molar is like a mill.

s0084: Know the life cycles of animals and plants, put stages in order, and understand why reproduction matters for the survival of a species
s0085:
How does a frog come from an egg in a pond?
TIMSS: 61% of fourth graders answered correctly
s0086: [1] In spring, tiny eggs appear in a pond, and a month later little frogs are hopping there. How does this happen? [2] In the international TIMSS study, on average 61 percent of fourth-grade students around the world answered questions on this topic correctly. Many students did well on this topic. Today you will learn to answer these questions with ease!
s0088:
Life cycle: birth → growth → reproduction
Then the new generation repeats the cycle
s0089: [1] Every living organism is born, grows, becomes an adult, and produces offspring like itself. This is called a life cycle. [2] The new generation follows the same path, so we call it a circle — a cycle.
s0090: Animals whose young look like their parents
s0091:
Chicken: egg → chick → chicken
Cat: kitten → adult cat
s0092: [1] The young of some animals look like their parents when they are born and simply grow bigger. A chick looks like a hen. [2] Mammals give birth to live young. A kitten also looks like an adult cat, only small.
s0094:
Frog: egg → tadpole → tadpole with legs → frog
The tadpole grows legs and loses its tail
Butterfly: egg → caterpillar → pupa → butterfly
s0095: [1] A frog lays eggs in water. A tadpole hatches from the egg; it swims with its tail like a fish and breathes with gills. [2] Little by little, the tadpole grows legs, its tail shrinks and disappears, and it becomes a frog with lungs. [3] A butterfly lays eggs, and a caterpillar hatches from each egg. The caterpillar eats a lot and grows, then turns into a pupa, and a butterfly comes out of the pupa.
s0097:
Seed → seedling → plant → flower → fruit, seeds
Reproduction needs a male and a female
No reproduction — the species dies out
s0098: [1] A plant sprouts from a seed, becomes a seedling, grows, flowers, and forms fruit. The fruit contains new seeds. [2] Many animals need a male and a female to reproduce. The young get features from their parents. [3] If animals cannot reproduce, the old ones age and die, and no new ones are born. The species dies out completely.
s0099:
Put in order: pupa, egg, butterfly, caterpillar
The start — egg
Egg → caterpillar → pupa → butterfly
s0100: [1] Example one. Write the stages of a butterfly's life cycle in the correct order: pupa, egg, butterfly, caterpillar. [2] Everything starts with the egg. A caterpillar hatches from the egg. [3] The caterpillar turns into a pupa, and a butterfly comes out of the pupa. The butterfly lays eggs again, and the cycle starts over.
s0102: [1] Compare: a chicken's life cycle has no pupa. As soon as a chick hatches from the egg, it looks like a hen and simply grows bigger.
s0103:
Only female foxes are left on an island
No males → no young are born
The rest grow old → foxes disappear from the island
s0104: [1] Example two is a reasoning question. On an island, only female foxes are left; there are no males. What will their future be? [2] Foxes need a male and a female to reproduce. Without males, no new fox cubs will be born. [3] Over time, the foxes that are there will grow old and die. So the foxes on this island will disappear completely.
s0105: There are tadpoles in the pond → a frog laid eggs
s0106: [1] In the same way: if tadpoles appear in a new pond, it means a frog came there and laid eggs. Tadpoles do not appear out of nowhere.

s0108: [1] What animal does a tadpole grow into? Write one word.

[2] If an animal's young do not look like the adult — for example, a caterpillar and a butterfly — then the animal changes shape. s0116: [1] Remember: every organism is born, grows, and reproduces. [2] The young of frogs and butterflies do not look like the adults; they change shape as they grow up. [3] Thanks to reproduction, a species does not die out. You did a wonderful job today!

s0122: Draw a circle: a tree grows from a seed, and the tree produces seeds again. The circle is closed — that is a cycle.

s0156: Explain how animals and plants are adapted to their environment, using examples of body structure and behavior
s0157:
Why doesn't a walrus freeze on the ice?
TIMSS: 61% of fourth graders answered correctly
s0158: [1] A walrus in the far north lies on the ice, but it does not feel cold. Why? [2] In the international TIMSS study, on average 61 percent of fourth-grade students around the world answered questions on this topic correctly. Questions about bird migration and desert animals were harder. Today you will learn to answer these questions with ease!
s0160:
Adaptation — a feature that helps an organism survive
Body structure: thick fat, fur, spines
Behavior: being active at night, migrating
s0161: [1] An adaptation is a feature or behavior that helps an organism survive in its environment. [2] Some adaptations are in the body: a thick layer of fat, thick fur, spines. [3] Others are in behavior: an animal hides during the day or flies to a warm region in winter.
s0163:
Walrus, seal: thick fat under the skin
Desert animals hide during the day
Camel: survives a long time on little water
Cactus: leaves — spines, the stem stores water
s0164: [1] Walruses and seals have a thick layer of fat under their skin. It keeps heat in, just like a thick jacket. [2] In the desert it is very hot during the day. Many desert animals stay in their burrows during the day and look for food at night, when the air is cool. [3] A camel can go a long time without drinking water, and the fat in its hump helps it survive without food. [4] A cactus's leaves have become spines, so it loses little water. It stores water in its thick stem.
s0166:
Hedgehog: rolls into a spiny ball when in danger
Duck: webbed feet — for swimming
Eagle: sharp talons — for catching prey
s0167: [1] When a hedgehog senses danger, it curls up into a spiny ball. A predator cannot bite it. [2] Birds' feet suit the places where they live: a duck has webbing between its toes and paddles through the water like an oar. [3] An eagle needs its sharp, curved talons to hold its prey tightly.
s0169:
Birds fly to warm regions in winter
A bird sits on its eggs to keep them warm
Pupil of the eye: gets bigger in the dark
s0170: [1] In winter it is cold, and there are fewer insects and fruits. That is why many birds fly away in the fall to warm regions where there is plenty of food. [2] A bird sits on its eggs and warms them with its body. A chick develops inside the warm egg. [3] Our eyes adapt too: in the dark the pupil gets bigger to let in more light, and in bright light it gets smaller.
s0171:
Which bird lives on water: look at its feet
Webbing → pushes water like an oar
Answer: near water, swims (duck, goose)
s0172: [1] Example one. A bird has webbing between its toes. Where does it live? [2] The webbing pushes the water like an oar and helps the bird swim. [3] So this bird swims in water, for example a duck or a goose.
s0173: Eagle's foot: sharp talons → catches prey
s0174: [1] Compare: an eagle's foot has no webbing, but it has sharp talons. It does not swim; it hunts prey.
s0175:
The desert mouse comes out at night. Why?
Daytime: hot, the body loses water
At night it is cool → water is saved
Answer: to avoid the heat and save water
s0176: [1] Example two, a reasoning question. A desert mouse stays in its burrow during the day and comes out only at night. What is the reason? [2] During the day the temperature in the desert is very high. In the heat an animal loses a lot of water, and there is little water in the desert. [3] At night the air is cool, so the animal loses less water and can look for food safely. [4] Answer: desert animals are active at night because they avoid the daytime heat and save the water in their bodies.
s0177: Cactus too: spiny leaves → loses little water
s0178: [1] Plants are adapted in the same way: a desert cactus saves water with its spiny leaves.
s0179: What protects a walrus from the cold?
s0180: [1] What protects a walrus from the cold in icy water? Write one or two words.

s0183: [1] You walked from a bright place into a dark room. Does the pupil of your eye get bigger or smaller? Write one word.

2) Find the problem: cold, lack of water, predators
3) How does the feature solve that problem?
s0186: [1] First, identify what kind of environment the animal lives in: cold, hot, desert, or water. [2] Then think: What difficulty is there in this environment? Is it cold, is there little water, are there predators? [3] Finally, connect the feature to the problem. Use the word “because” in your answer.
s0187:
Adaptation — a feature for survival
In the body: fat, fur, spines, webbed feet
In behavior: active at night, migrating, warming eggs
s0188: [1] Remember: an adaptation helps an organism survive in its environment. [2] It can be in the body: fat, fur, spines, webbed feet. [3] Or in behavior: being active at night, migrating to warm regions, warming eggs. Great work!
s0189: Adaptation = a feature that suits the environment
s0190: Every animal has a “tool” that suits the place where it lives. That is an adaptation.
s0191: In winter you dress warmly too
s0192: In winter you wear a thick jacket, and in summer a light shirt. Animals are also adapted to the cold with thick fur or fat.
s0194: Three steps: what the environment is like, what problem there is, and which feature of the animal solves it.
s0195:
Cold → fat, fur
Hot → coming out at night, saving water
s0196: In the cold, fat and fur keep an animal warm. In the hot desert, animals come out at night and save water.
s0197: Kyzylkum: quiet by day, alive at night
s0198: In the Kyzylkum Desert, everything is quiet during the day, and the animals are in their burrows. At night, snakes, mice, and hedgehogs come out looking for food.
s0199: Experiment: a fat-filled glove in icy water
s0200: If you put a glove filled with fat on one hand and dip it into icy water, that hand gets less cold. A walrus's fat works the same way.
s0201: Spines — protection, webbing — swimming, talons — grabbing
s0202: Spines give protection, webbed feet help with swimming, and sharp talons help with catching prey.
s0203: The fox could not bite the hedgehog
s0204: A hungry fox saw a hedgehog. The hedgehog curled up into a spiny ball. The fox pricked its nose and went away.
s0206: Imagine a bird's foot as a tool: a duck's foot is an oar, and an eagle's foot is a hook.

s0208: In winter there is not enough food for birds, so they fly to warm places.
s0209: Storks fly south in the fall and return in spring
s0210: In the fall, storks fly away to warm lands in the south, and in spring they return to their nests.

s0228: Build and read food chains; understand predator–prey relationships, where plants get their energy, and human impact
s0229:
Grass → rabbit → fox: who eats whom?
TIMSS: 56% of fourth graders answered correctly
s0230: [1] Grass grows in a field, a rabbit eats the grass, and a fox hunts the rabbit. How do we read this chain? [2] In the international TIMSS study, on average 56 percent of fourth-grade students around the world answered questions on this topic correctly. Questions about animals dying out were the hardest. Today you will learn to answer these questions with ease!
s0232:
Sun → plant: makes food
The plant uses energy to grow and live
Animals get food by eating other living things
s0233: [1] Green plants make their own food with the help of sunlight. That is why they are called producers. [2] A plant uses this energy to grow, put out new leaves, flower, and make seeds. [3] Animals cannot make their own food; they get energy by eating plants or other animals.
s0235:
Grass → grasshopper → frog → snake
Arrow points from “eaten” → “eater”
Herbivore — eats plants; predator — hunts animals
s0236: [1] A food chain shows who eats whom. A chain always starts with a plant. [2] The arrow points from the one that is eaten to the one that eats it. In other words, it shows where the energy goes. [3] An animal that eats plants is a herbivore, and one that hunts and eats other animals is a predator. An animal that is hunted is called prey.
s0238:
If one link changes, the others change too
Fewer foxes → more rabbits → less grass
s0239: [1] The animals in a chain depend on each other. If the number of one changes, the numbers of the others change too. [2] For example, if there are fewer foxes, fewer animals hunt the rabbits, and the rabbits multiply. And many rabbits eat a lot of grass.
s0241:
Causes of extinction: habitat loss, hunting
Pollution also does harm
Protection: nature reserves, bicycles, buses
s0242: [1] The main reasons animals die out are habitat loss when forests are cut down, and too much hunting. [2] Air and water pollution also harm plants and animals. [3] We can protect nature: creating nature reserves and using a bicycle or bus instead of a car pollute the air less.
s0243:
Chain: leaf → caterpillar → sparrow → hawk
The caterpillar eats the leaf → herbivore
The sparrow and hawk eat animals → predators
s0244: [1] Example one. We made a chain from a leaf, a caterpillar, a sparrow, and a hawk. Find the predators here. [2] The caterpillar eats the leaf, so it is a herbivore. [3] The sparrow hunts the caterpillar, and the hawk hunts the sparrow. So both are predators, and the hawk is at the end of the chain.
s0245: Leaf — producer, the start of the chain
s0246: [1] The leaf at the start of the chain makes food from sunlight; it is a producer. The energy of all the animals starts with it.
s0247:
Grass → rabbit → fox. All the foxes were hunted
Step 1: nobody hunts the rabbits → they multiply
Step 2: many rabbits → less grass
Step 3: not enough grass → rabbits decrease too
s0248: [1] Example two, a reasoning question. In one area, people hunted all the foxes. What happens next? [2] Step one: now nobody hunts the rabbits, so their number goes up. [3] Step two: many rabbits eat a lot of grass, and the grass runs low. [4] Step three: when there is not enough food, the rabbits go hungry, and later their number goes down too. See, everything is connected!
s0249: Conclusion: if one species disappears, the balance is upset
s0250: [1] You see, the loss of one species changed the whole chain. That is why we must protect the balance of nature.

Energy: Sun → plants → animals

s0260: [1] Remember: energy passes from the Sun to plants, and from plants to animals. [2] The arrow points from the one that is eaten to the one that eats it. [3] Every living organism in the chain is important, and we must protect them. Well done!

s0262: A plant gets its energy from the Sun, while an animal gets it by eating food.
s0263: The flower on the windowsill grew toward the sun
s0264: The flower by your window stretched toward the sun. It made food with the help of light and put out new leaves.

s0270: An aphid sucks the sap of a rose leaf in your garden, and a ladybug eats the aphid. This is a food chain in the garden.

s0301:
Why is drinking milk good for your bones?
TIMSS: 41% of fourth graders answered correctly
s0302: [1] Your mother says, “Drink your milk, and your bones will be strong.” Is that true? Today we will find out. [2] In the international TIMSS study, on average 41 percent of fourth-grade students around the world answered questions on this topic correctly. This topic is considered quite difficult, especially the question about calcium. Today you will learn to answer these questions with ease!
s0304:
Calcium — makes bones and teeth strong
Sources of calcium: milk, yogurt, cheese, cottage cheese
Protein — growth; fruits, vegetables — vitamins
s0305: [1] Calcium makes our bones and teeth strong. A growing child needs especially a lot of it. [2] Milk and milk products have the most calcium: yogurt, cheese, cottage cheese. [3] Meat, eggs, and beans are rich in protein, which helps the body grow. Fruits and vegetables contain vitamins.
s0307:
The flu — caused by a virus
Spread: coughing, sneezing, dirty hands
Protection: washing hands with soap, covering your mouth
s0308: [1] The flu is an infectious disease. It is caused by a virus, which is so tiny it cannot be seen. [2] When a sick person coughs or sneezes, the virus spreads through the air. It also spreads through dirty hands and shared dishes. [3] To protect ourselves, we wash our hands with soap, and when we sneeze, we cover our mouth and nose with a tissue or our elbow.
s0310:
Healthy body temperature — about 36.6 °C
When running: the body warms up, the heart beats fast
When we rest, it slowly returns to normal
High temperature for a long time — a sign of illness
s0311: [1] A healthy person's body temperature is about thirty-six point six degrees. We measure it with a thermometer. [2] When we run or play, our muscles work, the body warms up, the heart beats faster, and breathing speeds up. [3] When we rest, our temperature, heartbeat, and breathing slowly return to how they were before. [4] If a person's temperature rises well above 37 degrees even while sitting quietly, this is a fever — a sign of illness.
s0312:
Which is richest in calcium: an apple, bread, or cheese?
Calcium — in milk products
Answer: cheese (it is made from milk)
s0313: [1] Example one. An apple, bread, and cheese — which is richest in calcium? [2] Let's remember: there is the most calcium in milk products. [3] Cheese is made from milk, so the answer is cheese.
s0314: Also rich in calcium: yogurt, cottage cheese, sesame
s0315: [1] Yogurt, cottage cheese, and sesame seeds also have a lot of calcium. Drinking a glass of milk or yogurt every day is good for you.
s0316:
Ali ran for 10 minutes: 36.6 °C → 37.2 °C
Reason: his working muscles gave off heat
Not sick: when he rests, his temperature drops
s0317: [1] Example two, a reasoning question. Ali ran for ten minutes, and his temperature rose from thirty-six point six to thirty-seven point two degrees. Why? [2] When we run, our muscles work hard and give off heat. That is why the body warms up a little. [3] This is not an illness. When Ali rests, he sweats, and his temperature returns to normal.
s0318: If it is 38 °C while sitting quietly — a fever
s0319: [1] But if Ali had been sitting quietly and his temperature was thirty-eight degrees, that would be a fever. Then he should see a doctor.

s0367: Understand the solid, liquid, and gas states of matter, changes of state, solutions and mixtures, and the properties of materials
s0368:
Ice, water, and steam — one substance!
TIMSS: 46% of fourth graders answered correctly
s0369: [1] The ice in the freezer, the water in a glass, and the steam from a teapot are all one substance: water. How can that be? [2] In the international TIMSS study, on average 46 percent of fourth-grade students around the world answered questions on this topic correctly. Questions about identifying a gas and about condensation were the hardest. Today you will learn to answer these questions with ease!
s0371:
Solid: shape and volume do not change
Liquid: has a volume, takes the shape of its container
Gas: fills the whole container
s0372: [1] A solid — for example, ice or a stone — keeps its own shape and volume. [2] A liquid — for example, water or milk — flows and takes the shape of whatever container we pour it into, but its volume does not change. [3] A gas has neither its own shape nor its own volume; it fills the whole container. Air and water vapor are gases. Often they cannot be seen.
s0374:
Heating: ice → water (melting) → vapor (evaporation)
Cooling: vapor → water (condensation) → ice
Water freezes at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C
Drops on a cold window — condensation
s0375: [1] If we heat ice, it melts and turns into water. If we heat the water further, it evaporates and turns into a gas. [2] If we cool water vapor, it turns into drops of water — this is condensation. If we cool water, it freezes. [3] Pure water freezes at zero degrees and boils at one hundred degrees. [4] The drops that appear on the outside of a cold glass form from water vapor in the air. This is condensation too.
s0377:
Salt dissolves in water — you can't see it, but it is there
Fine salt, hot water, stirring — faster
Mixture: sand + water, rice + beans
s0378: [1] If we put salt in water and stir, it dissolves and can no longer be seen. But the salt does not disappear: the water tastes salty. [2] Fine salt dissolves faster than coarse salt. Hot water and stirring also make it dissolve faster. [3] In a mixture, several substances are together, and they can be separated. For example, we separate sandy water by filtering it.
s0380:
Same size — different weight
Ice floats in water: most of it is underwater
A magnet attracts iron; wood and paper burn
s0381: [1] If we take a brick, an apple, and a piece of foam of the same size, the brick is the heaviest and the foam is the lightest. [2] Ice is lighter than water, so it floats. But most of it is underwater, and only a small part sticks out on top. [3] A magnet attracts iron objects but does not attract aluminum or copper. Paper and wood burn; stone and glass do not.
s0382:
Ice, water, steam — order by temperature
Ice ≤ 0 °C, water — from 0 to 100 °C
Steam ≈ 100 °C → ice < water < steam
s0383: [1] Example one. Ice, water, and the steam from boiling water — which is the hottest, and which is the coldest? [2] Ice is at zero degrees or colder. Liquid water is between zero and one hundred degrees. [3] The steam from boiling water is about one hundred degrees. So the coldest is ice, and the hottest is steam.
s0385: [1] That is why, when we heat ice, it turns first into water and then into steam. At each stage we add heat.
s0386:
Water in the glass: 200 g, salt: 20 g
The salt dissolved and could no longer be seen
The salt did not disappear — it spread through the water
$200 + 20 = 220$ g
s0387: [1] Example two, a reasoning question. Laylo weighed the water in a glass on a scale — two hundred grams — and the salt separately — twenty grams. [2] Then she put the salt in the water and dissolved it. The salt could no longer be seen. If we weigh it now, what will the scale show? [3] The salt did not disappear; it broke up into tiny particles and spread through the water. That is why the water is salty. [4] So the mass of the solution is two hundred twenty grams. Mass does not change when something dissolves.
s0388: If we evaporate the water, the salt stays at the bottom
s0389: [1] Here is more proof that the salt did not disappear: if we heat the solution and evaporate the water, white salt is left at the bottom of the container.
s0390: What state is the steam that forms when water boils?
s0391: [1] When water boils, what state is the water vapor that forms: solid, liquid, or gas? Remember, the white cloud above a teapot is made of tiny droplets that formed from the vapor.
s0393: 10 g of sugar was dissolved in 100 g of water. Mass = ? g
s0394: [1] We put ten grams of sugar into one hundred grams of water and dissolved it. What is the mass of the solution in grams? Write only the number.

s0399: [1] Remember: matter can be solid, liquid, or gas. [2] Heating causes melting and evaporation; cooling causes freezing and condensation. [3] When something dissolves, it does not disappear, and its mass is conserved. You're great!

s0441: Understand light sources, reflection and shadows, heat transfer and conductors, electric circuits, and how magnets interact
s0442:
Why does a light bulb light up, and why do shadows form?
TIMSS: 54% of fourth graders answered correctly
s0443: [1] In the evening you turn on the light — the room gets bright, and your shadow appears on the wall. All of this has to do with energy. [2] In the international TIMSS study, on average 54 percent of fourth-grade students around the world answered questions on this topic correctly. Questions about light bulb circuits and magnets were the hardest. Today you will learn to answer these questions with ease!
s0445:
Light sources: the Sun, a lamp, fire
The Moon and mirrors reflect light
White light is made of the colors of the rainbow
s0446: [1] Things that give off their own light are called light sources: the Sun, a lamp that is on, a fire, a candle. [2] The Moon does not shine by itself; it reflects sunlight. Mirrors and the still water of a lake also reflect light. [3] The Sun's white light is actually made up of seven colors. We see these colors in a rainbow after the rain.
s0448:
Light travels in straight lines
A shadow is on the side of the object opposite the source
s0449: [1] Light travels in straight lines and cannot pass through an opaque object. [2] The object blocks the light, and a shadow forms behind it, that is, on the side opposite the light source.
s0451:
Heat moves from hot to cold
Metal conducts heat well, wood poorly
s0452: [1] Heat always moves from a hot object to a colder one. If we put a spoon in hot tea, the spoon gets hot. [2] Metal conducts heat well, so a metal spoon heats up quickly. Wood and plastic conduct heat poorly.
s0454:
Circuit: battery + wires + bulb
If the circuit is closed, the bulb lights up
Metal conducts; plastic and rubber do not
s0455: [1] A simple electric circuit is made of a battery, wires, and a light bulb. The battery is the source of electrical energy. [2] For current to flow, the circuit must be an unbroken, closed loop. The bulb's two contact points are connected to the two ends of the battery. [3] Metals such as copper and iron conduct electricity. Plastic, rubber, and wood do not conduct electricity; they are insulators.
s0457:
A magnet has two poles: N and S
Like poles repel, unlike poles attract
An iron paper clip is attracted to a magnet
s0458: [1] Every magnet has two poles: north, N, and south, S. [2] The like poles of two magnets, for example N and N, push each other away. Unlike poles, N and S, attract each other. [3] A magnet attracts an iron paper clip. A paper clip stuck to a magnet can become a temporary magnet itself and attract another paper clip.
s0459:
The Sun is on the left. Where is the tree's shadow?
The shadow is on the side opposite the source
Answer: on the right
s0460: [1] Example one. In the evening, the Sun is to the left of a tree. Which side does the tree's shadow fall on? [2] Let's remember: a shadow is on the side opposite the light source. [3] So if the Sun is on the left, the shadow falls on the right side of the tree.
s0461:
Circuit: battery, bulb, 2 wires, and a ruler
Plastic does not conduct → the circuit is broken
A copper spoon instead of the ruler → it lights up
s0462: [1] Example two, a reasoning question. A circuit has a battery, a bulb, and two wires, and a plastic ruler is placed between the wires. Will the bulb light up? [2] Plastic does not conduct electricity, so the circuit is broken. The bulb will not light up. [3] If we put a metal spoon in place of the ruler, current will flow and the bulb will light up.
s0463: Two carts: their N poles face each other
s0464: [1] One more situation: magnets are placed on two carts with their N poles facing each other. If we push them close together and let go, they move away from each other in opposite directions.
s0465: To light the bulb: a rubber band or a copper wire?
s0466: [1] You can put a rubber band or a copper wire in the gap in the circuit. With which one will the bulb light up? Write one word.
s0468: If S and S poles come close, do they attract?
s0469: [1] We brought the S and S poles of two magnets close together. Do they attract or repel? Write one word.

s0521: Understand force as a push or a pull, gravity, friction, and wind force, and analyze balance on a scale and a seesaw
s0522:
Why does an apple fall down and not up?
TIMSS: 60% of fourth graders answered correctly
s0523: [1] An apple that comes off a tree always falls down. What pulls it? [2] In the international TIMSS study, on average 60 percent of fourth-grade students around the world answered questions on this topic correctly. Reasoning questions about balance on a scale and a seesaw were harder. Today you will learn to answer these questions with ease!
s0525:
Force — a push or a pull
A force starts or stops motion
A force changes direction and shape
s0526: [1] A force is a push or a pull. We use force when we open a door and when we pull a cart. [2] A force can make something at rest start moving or make something moving stop. [3] A force can change the direction of motion; for example, you kick a ball and change its direction. If you press modeling clay, its shape changes.
s0528:
Earth pulls everything toward itself
That is why things fall down
s0529: [1] Earth pulls everything toward its center. This pulling force is called gravity. [2] That is why a pencil you drop falls down and does not fly up.
s0531:
Friction slows motion down
Ice — smooth (little friction), sand — rough
Wind pushes the sail — the boat moves
s0532: [1] When two surfaces touch and slide against each other, friction appears. It slows motion down. [2] There is little friction on smooth ice, so we slip. There is a lot of friction on a rough surface. [3] Wind is a force too: it pushes the sail, and the sailboat moves.
s0534:
Balance scale: the heavier pan goes down
Pans level — the weights are equal
Seesaw: the heavier child sits closer to the middle — balance
s0535: [1] On a balance scale, the pan with the heavier object goes down, and the pan with the lighter one goes up. [2] If the two pans are level, the objects on both sides weigh the same. [3] On a seesaw for two, the heavier child goes down. For balance, the heavier child should sit closer to the pivot.
s0536:

The lower pan is heavier
Answer: the apple is heavier than the pear
s0537: [1] Example one. There is an apple on the left pan of a scale and a pear on the right. The left pan went down. Which one is heavier? [2] The object on the pan that went down is heavier. [3] So the apple is heavier than the pear.
s0538: If the pans are level, the weights are equal
s0539: [1] If the pans stopped level, the apple and the pear would weigh the same.

Where does drinking water come from?
TIMSS: 42% of fourth graders answered correctly
s0596: [1] When you turn on the tap, clean water flows. Where does this water come from, and why should we save it? [2] In the international TIMSS study, on average 42 percent of fourth-grade students around the world answered questions on this topic correctly. This topic was quite difficult, especially the questions about using air and the energy of a waterfall. Today you will learn to answer these questions with ease!
s0598:
Most of Earth's surface is covered by water
Most water is salty; there is little fresh water
Fresh water: rivers, lakes, glaciers, underground
s0599: [1] Most of Earth's surface — more than about two thirds — is water: oceans and seas. [2] But almost all of this water is salty. There is very little fresh water that is fit to drink. [3] Fresh water is found in rivers, lakes, glaciers, and underground. Drinking water is cleaned and comes to our homes through pipes.
s0601:
Soil: small rocks, sand, clay, and humus
Soil rich in humus — the most fertile
Sand lets water through fast, clay holds it
Wind and water wear soil away
s0602: [1] Soil is made of tiny pieces of rock, sand, clay, and humus. Humus is rotted plant and animal remains. [2] The best soil for plants is dark soil rich in humus. It has a lot of nutrients and holds water well. [3] Sandy soil lets water through quickly, while clay soil holds water. [4] In nature, wind and rainwater wash or blow soil away. This wearing away is called erosion.
s0604:
Air: breathing, burning, wind energy
Water: drinking, irrigation, making electricity
We save water: we turn off the tap
s0605: [1] We need air to breathe, and fire burns using the oxygen in the air. Wind turns wind turbines and gives us electricity. [2] We drink water and use it to irrigate crops. At a hydroelectric power station, electricity is produced by the force of water falling from a waterfall or a dam. [3] To save water, we turn off the tap while brushing our teeth, get dripping taps fixed, and do not stay in the shower for a long time.
s0607:
Renewable: the Sun, wind, flowing water
Nonrenewable: coal, oil, gas
s0608: [1] Sunlight, wind, and flowing water do not run out. They are renewable resources. [2] Coal, oil, and natural gas formed over millions of years. If we use them up, they are gone, so they are nonrenewable resources.
s0609:

Advantage: water for irrigation is close by

s0610: [1] Example one. Farmers often plant crops along a river. What is the advantage of this? [2] Water for irrigating the crops is close by. Besides, the silt brought by the river makes the soil fertile. [3] There is also a disadvantage: if the river floods in spring, the water may wash away the crops and flood homes.
s0611: Protection: a levee is built along the river
s0612: [1] To protect themselves from floods, people build an earth wall, a levee, along the river.

s0669: [1] The water in a puddle disappears in the sun, then clouds appear and it rains. Where does this water go, and where does it come back from? [2] In the international TIMSS study, on average 37 percent of fourth-grade students around the world answered questions on this topic correctly. This was one of the hardest topics, especially the question about fossils. Today you will learn to answer these questions with ease!
s0671:
Weather: temperature, precipitation, wind, clouds
Thermometer — temperature, wind vane — wind direction
Rain gauge — how much rain fell
s0672: [1] Weather is the condition of the air at a certain place and time: temperature, precipitation, wind, and clouds. [2] We measure temperature with a thermometer. A wind vane shows which direction the wind is blowing from. [3] We find out how much rain fell with a rain gauge.
s0674:
1) Evaporation: the Sun heats water → vapor
2) Condensation: vapor cools → clouds
3) Precipitation: drops → rain, snow
4) Water flows back to rivers and seas
s0675: [1] The Sun heats the water in seas, lakes, and rivers. The water evaporates and rises into the air as invisible vapor. [2] High up, the air is cold. The vapor cools and turns into tiny droplets, which together form clouds. This is condensation. [3] When the droplets grow bigger and heavier, they fall to the ground as rain or snow. [4] Water that falls on the ground flows through rivers to the sea or soaks into the ground. Then it all starts over again.
s0677:
A river flows from high ground to low ground
It starts in the mountains and flows to the lowlands
s0678: [1] A river always flows from higher ground to lower ground, because Earth's gravity pulls the water down. [2] Rivers start from melting snow and glaciers in the mountains and flow down to low plains, to a lake or the sea.
s0680:
Fossil — a trace of an ancient living thing turned to stone
Fossils formed millions of years ago
Lower layer — older
s0681: [1] A fossil is the trace or remains of a plant or animal that lived very long ago, preserved in rock. [2] Many fossils come from organisms that lived millions of years ago. Turning to stone takes a very long time. [3] Rocks lie in layers. Usually a lower layer formed earlier, so a fossil in it is older.
s0682:

s0683: [1] Example one. Put the stages of the water cycle in order: precipitation, evaporation, cloud formation. [2] First, the Sun heats the water and evaporates it. [3] The vapor cools and forms clouds, and precipitation falls from the clouds. The correct order is evaporation, clouds, precipitation.
s0684: The Sun's energy drives the cycle
s0685: [1] The Sun's energy drives this whole cycle: if the Sun did not heat the water, there would be no evaporation.

[2] Shellfish live only in seawater; they cannot climb a mountain by themselves. [3] So very long ago, millions of years ago, this place was the bottom of a sea. Later the layers of the earth rose up and formed a mountain.

s0741:
Why does night come after day?
TIMSS: 48% of fourth graders answered correctly
s0742: [1] Every morning the Sun rises, and every evening it sets. Is this because the Sun moves, or is there another reason? [2] In the international TIMSS study, on average 48 percent of fourth-grade students around the world answered questions on this topic correctly. Explaining the cause of day and night was the hardest question. Today you will learn to answer these questions with ease!
s0743:
The Sun — a star at the center of the system
8 planets orbit the Sun
The Moon — Earth's satellite
The Sun gives Earth light and heat
s0744: [1] The Sun is a star. It gives off its own light and heat and is at the center of the solar system. [2] Eight planets orbit the Sun. Earth is the third planet from the Sun. [3] The Moon orbits Earth; it is Earth's natural satellite. The Moon is about four times smaller than Earth. [4] The Sun gives Earth light and heat. Without it, plants would not grow, and there would be no life on Earth.
s0746:
Earth spins on its axis
One full turn — 24 hours
The side facing the Sun — day, the other side — night
s0747: [1] Earth spins on its axis like a top. [2] It takes Earth about twenty-four hours, or one full day, to make one complete turn. [3] It is day on the side of Earth facing the Sun and night on the opposite side. The Sun does not go around Earth!
s0749:
Earth goes around the Sun in 1 year
The cause of the seasons — the tilt of Earth's axis
s0750: [1] It takes Earth one year, or about three hundred sixty-five days, to go once around the Sun. [2] Earth's axis is slightly tilted. That is why in summer the Sun's rays hit us more directly and the days are long, and in winter it is the opposite.
s0752:
The Moon does not shine by itself — it reflects sunlight
The Moon goes around Earth in about 1 month
s0753: [1] The Moon does not give off its own light. What we see on the Moon is reflected sunlight. [2] The Moon goes around Earth in about one month. During this time, the Moon's shape seems to change: new moon, half moon, full moon.
s0754:

On the opposite side — night
s0755: [1] Example one. It is lunchtime, daytime, in Tashkent. What is happening at the same moment in America, on the opposite side of Earth? [2] Earth is shaped like a ball, and the Sun lights up only one half of it. [3] If Tashkent is on the side facing the Sun, America is on the opposite side. So it is night there.
s0756: After half a day, everything switches
s0757: [1] Earth keeps spinning. After about half a day, Tashkent will be on the side facing away from the Sun, and night will begin there.

s0759: [1] Example two, a reasoning question. A picture shows three balls: a large one, a medium one, and a small one.
